{{Short description|British geodesist (1920–2002)}}
{{Use British English|date=November 2017}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2024}}

'''Alwyn Rudolph Robbins''' (5 January 1920 – 9 or 10 January 2002) was a British [[geodesist]], former chairman of the [[Royal Society]] subcommittee on geodesy, and a founding fellow of [[St Cross College, Oxford|St Cross College]] at the [[University of Oxford]]. Robbins published on [[geodesy]] and [[photogrammetry]], with additional contributions to [[geodetic astronomy]] and the development of [[clock]]s. He held multiple positions within the [[International Association of Geodesy]] during his career as well.

==Early life, education, and military service==
Alwyn Robbins was born in [[Lydney]], Gloucestershire on 5 January 1920.{{efn|Sources conflict on Robbins' place of birth, with both Lydney and [[Oxford]] put forward.<ref name="Ashkenazi Lydney"/><ref name="Survey Review Oxford"/> His date of birth is calculated from his age at death.<ref name="Survey Review DoB"/>}} He was educated at [[Blundell's School]] in [[Tiverton, Devon|Tiverton]], Devon, winning multiple [[scholarship]]s and [[exhibition (scholarship)|exhibitions]] to attend [[Hertford College, Oxford|Hertford College]] of the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name="Ashkenazi Blundells"/> At Hertford, he studied mathematics,<ref name="Olliver Blundells"/> and participated in [[rowing]], [[squash (sport)|squash]], and [[tennis]].<ref name="Ashkenazi sports"/>

Robbins graduated from Oxford in 1940,{{efn|Olliver 2002 states that Robbins did not complete his degree until after his return from military service,<ref name="Olliver RE"/> but other sources offer that his graduation occurred before mobilisation.}} and was awarded his degree with [[first class honours]].<ref name="Ashkenazi degree"/><ref name="Survey Review degree"/> Later that year, he received a [[commission (document)|commission]] in the Survey Branch of the [[Royal Engineers]] and was posted to [[West Africa]].

From his studies at Oxford, Robbins had also received [[Master of Science]], [[Master of Arts]], and [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degrees.<ref name="Survey Review degrees"/>

==Career==
Following military demobilisation in 1946, Robbins returned to Oxford and soon gained a post as an academic post in surveying.<ref name="Survey Review demobilised"/> He was promoted multiple times and continued to climb the ranks, becoming a [[reader (academic rank)|reader]] and head of the surveying and geodesy department in 1966 upon the retirement of [[Guy Bomford]].<ref name="Ashkenazi reader"/><ref name="Olliver Bomford"/> {{harvnb|Olliver|2002}} records:

{{quote|His work for his [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] degree (converted to [[Master of Science|MSc]]) involved developing precise formulae for the geometry of long lines on the [[earth ellipsoid]]. His [[Doctor of Philosophy|D.Phil.]] project was an investigation of the shape of the [[geoid]] – the [[equipotential surface]] of the Earth's gravity field that coincides with the sea surface{{snd}}in England and Scotland. This involved making astronomical observations at 43 [[Ordnance Survey]] [[triangulation point]]s, extending from [[Dover]] to [[John o'Groats]]{{snd}}an arduous campaign over several seasons that had to be fitted in with his academic duties. His particular interest in astronomy was the definition and precise measurement of time, and he designed a highly accurate portable printing [[Clock|chronometer]] for use in geodetic astronomy, which was successfully marketed. He was also the author of a military handbook on the same subject.}}

Robbins published on geodesy and on timekeeping, and held several appointments within the [[International Association of Geodesy]]. He also represented the United Kingdom on the international scale as a delegate to conferences and assemblies, and was the chairman of the geodesy subcommittee of the [[Royal Society]].<ref name="Ashkenazi career"/> He also had extensive international connections and spent in various countries, as well as a two-year secondment with the [[Ministry of Defence (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Defence]].<ref name="Olliver links"/> During his time at Oxford, robbins held multiple visiting professorships, including at [[Ohio State University]], [[Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology]], and the [[University of Otago]].<ref name="Survey Review visiting"/>

In 1980, Robbins retired, becoming an ''[[emeritus]]'' fellow of St Cross College.<ref name="Olliver retirement"/> During his career, he had been elected [[Fellow of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors]], [[Fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society]], and [[Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society]].<ref name="Survey Review fellowships"/>

==Personal life and death==
Following his retirement, Robbins moved to Devon and pursued recreational [[fly-fishing]].<ref name="Olliver Devon"/> He died in his home at [[Ottery St Mary]]<ref name="Olliver died"/> on 9 or 10 January 2002.{{efn|Sources conflict on date of death: Olliver 2002<ref name="Olliver DoD"/> and ''Survey Review'' 2002 state he died on 9 January,<ref name="Survey Review DoD"/> while Ashkenazi 2002 and Ashkenazi & Lachapelle 2002 state he died on 10 January.<ref name="Ashkenazi DoD"/>}} He was survived by his wife Mary and his children: a son and a daughter, Mike and Rowena.<ref name="Olliver leaves"/><ref name="Ashkenazi missed"/>
